title: “The Invention of Love” is running through 10/3 at TheatreLab in NYC,...
transcript: Queerness in 19th century academia is the subject matter of this rarely revived play from the late, great Sir Tom Stoppard, maybe best known for Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead, and Shakespeare in love. And if you know, you know, this production stars New York theatre icon David Greenspan. It tells the story of the renowned English poet slash scholar A E. Hausman, who was closeted at a time when homosexuality was criminalized. With this play, Stoppard is doing what he always did better than anyone, which is taking the intellectual and finding the emotion in it. In this case, presenting Hausman's love for poetry, romance, and the Greek and Roman literature as an outlet to express his hidden longings. That also means, in true Stoppard fashion, it's extremely dense, even more than a lot of his work, to be honest, with these extended sequences of pretty esoteric academic discussions that were pretty hard to follow and digest. I'm tempted to criticize Stoppard for writing this in such a willfully opaque, almost inside-baseball way, but in fairness, I did ultimately get the gist of what was happening and what he was exploring thematically. Plus I said the same thing about Arcadia when I first saw it, and now it's like my favorite play of all time. Although that play inspired me to dig deeper into it in a way that I'm not sure this one did. More to the point, though, doing a play like this is a huge undertaking for a cast and director. And I'm not sure that this company was well-positioned to pull it off. At the early press performance I went to, it felt like the company was not struggling with the dialogue, but straining a little bit to get their mind and their mouths around it. It's not for lack of talent. I just get the sense that this play demands a more extended rehearsal period and preview period and run in general than they were able to give it. So on one hand, I question if this was the right play for them to pick under the circumstances. But at the same time, clearly no one else is stepping up to the plate to revive this play. And I do think it's worth reviving.
reasoning: Reviewer appreciates the play's themes and thinks it's worth reviving, but expresses significant reservations about the density of the writing and the production's execution, suggesting the cast wasn't quite ready.
